citations.narrative:
Multiple bird housing facilities are failing to protect the birds from injury, are not adequately restricting the entry of other
animals that may negatively affect the birds’ welfare, and are not securely containing the birds within their enclosures.
Within the last six months, there have been multiple incidents of missing or dead birds, presumed by the facility to be due
to predation or escape.
-In August 2026, a Catalina macaw was found missing from his enclosure in the morning, with only several feathers left
behind. The number and condition of the feathers suggested a struggle, but no body or other remains of the macaw were
found. The macaw was housed in a standard metal bird cage located inside a barn. During the summer, the barn windows
and one barn door are left open overnight to allow airflow. The licensee reported previously seeing and capturing several
raccoons and skunks inside the barn.
-In the Spring of 2026, 2 peacocks were found dead in their enclosure with their heads missing. A pigeon also went
missing from the same enclosure during that time period. The outdoor enclosure is constructed with metal wire over a
metal frame. There was a broken area of wire where a predator had gained access into the enclosure. The facility
patched and re-enforced the broken wire, however, in the same enclosure, during the current inspection, a male red-
golden pheasant could not be found. The licensee stated that she had seen the pheasant the day before. There was a
new area at the bottom of the enclosure where the wire had broken away from the frame and the structure had enough
flexibility for entrance/exit of a raccoon-sized predator.
Birds that disappear from their primary enclosure or that are not protected from predation may suffer from stress, injury, or
death. Correct by ensuring that bird enclosures are maintained in good repair, protect the birds from injury, contain the
birds, and restrict other animals from entering who may negatively affect the welfare of the birds within. Correct by 9/9/26

The licensee's records are missing the dates of disposal for several animals that have died in the last year, including a
Catalina Macaw, a juvenile rabbit, a pigeon, and 2 peacocks. The records are also missing a disposition for 9 Peach
doves, which the licensee states were donated.
Accurate and well-maintained records of acquisition and disposition of animals is critical to ensure a thorough inspection,
to rapidly identify and trace animals in a potential disease outbreak, to make sure all animals are accounted for, and to
verify animals at the facility receive adequate veterinary care. The license shall make, keep, and maintain records or
forms which fully and correctly disclose the information listed in 2.75(b)(1)(i)-(vii) concerning animals purchased or
otherwise acquired, owned, held, leased, or otherwise in his or her possession or under his or her control, or which is
transported, sold, euthanized, or otherwise disposed of by the licensee. The required information includes the date of
disposition. To be corrected from this day forward.

Multiple rabbit primary enclosures were not maintained in good repair and did not contain the animals.
-In the summer of 2026, one juvenile male Dutch rabbit escaped its enclosure when the enclosure was not properly
latched. The licensee reported attempting to catch the rabbit for several days, but was unsuccessful. The licensee
believes the rabbit was likely killed after several days without locating the rabbit and the number of raccoons and skunks
seen on facility grounds.
-Another rabbit is housed on the floor in a horse stall in the barn. The rabbit has dug a burrow under the cement floor of
the neighboring tack room. There is also a large gap, approximately 3ft x 6", under the opposite wall of the stall that would
allow the rabbit to escape or predators to gain access. The licensee states that she regularly sees the rabbit but has not
been able to capture it.
-In a rabbit enclosure housing a female and male adult Dutch rabbits, a wooden panel was found with multiple wood
staples protruding approximately .5" and leaving sharp points exposed.
When rabbits are able to escape their primary enclosures they are at increased risk of injury, predation, or death. In
addition, sharp points within rabbit enclosures can cause injury or even death to the animals. All primary enclosures shall
be maintained in good repair to protect the rabbits from injury, to contain them, and keep predators out. Correct by
September 9, 2026.

The primary enclosures housing a spider monkey did not contain the animal securely. The licensee reported that in the
spring of 2026, the spider monkey learned how to open and escape her enclosure and would wander the property.
Multiple latch types were attempted, but none were effective in preventing her escape. The licensee described one
incident in which the spider monkey made it off the property to a public road. Although the spider monkey was recovered
each time, the licensee ultimately decided to rehome her to prevent potential harm. Enclosures and containment
measures that are not adequate for the species involved can lead to escape. All primary enclosures must be constructed
and maintained so that they contain the nonhuman primates securely and prevent accidental opening of the enclosure,
including opening by the animal. Corrected prior to the time of inspection.

The Patagonian Cavy enclosure did not securely contain all cavies. During the inspection, an adult female Patagonian
cavy was observed sitting in the grass a few feet outside of its enclosure. A hole approximately 8 inches high by 6 inches
wide was identified in the fencing on the lower left corner of the gate to the cavy enclosure. The licensee put the adult
female cavy back into it's enclosure. Shortly after, the cavy was observed again at the open hole in the fencing. The
licensee then blocked the hole in the fence with a temporary barrier. When enclosures are not structurally sound or
maintained in good repair animals can escape and become injured or harmed by predators. The enclosure must be
constructed to be structurally sound, and maintained in good repair, to contain the animals and protect them from harm or
injury. The enclosure fencing must be repaired by September 9, 2026.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with a facility representative.
Additional Inspectors:
Tomeka Manson, VETERINARY MEDICAL OFFICER n
